One goes to Sekovici and one to Kladanj. That is what I said on the first occasion when I was asked about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you mention Mr. Beara's name to the investigator at the OTP when he interviewed you on 9 December 2004, as you've just testified?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I had seen him and I just said a minute ago that I saw the man in Han Pijesak that he saluted my commander and I said that he personally didn't issue any order of any of our soldiers when I was there. After I had gone I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify that you're not saying you saw Mr. Beara anywhere around the base or Vlasenica on the 15th, are you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At some other point in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you - that day on the 15th - organise any materials for any group to go out pursuant to what you'd heard and seen happen, to get a group to go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was customary when a unit goes out into the field for certain amount of ammunition and weapons to be prepared as support, if a unit is dispatched to carry out a mission. In addition to basic standard issue, machine -- submachine-gun can be added, a larger amount of ammunition may also be added depending on how long they are going to stay out in the field, also meals or sleeping bags, pads and stuff like that. All the materiel normally used whenever a unit is going into the field as a kind of backup supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that's generally what you do. In this particular situation, do you remember getting any materials, food or weapons or anything else, together for this group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe two zolja launchers, these are hand-held launchers. One PKT. And a crate of ammunition. I cannot say exactly but I think there was around 1200 rounds in each crate. These were rifle bullets. And also the other usual stuff like food, rations and water flasks and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's a PKT for us that may not know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's a submachine-gun, 7.62 millimetre, the latest version of 84 submachine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it sometimes called an M-84?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, M-84.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that's a bigger machine-gun than the automatic, normal automatic machine-gun that a soldier might have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this ammunition you mentioned, which weapon was this ammunition for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Since machine-guns are issued as necessary, there is always a crate of ammunition that goes with it. And it's already in -- they were always stashed in the belts. Plus a crate that is given to soldiers as kind of replenishment in case they get engaged in combat situations. It depends on the actual situation on the ground whether it's going to be used or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But you had mentioned specific -- I think you said 1200 rounds for a crate. Was that the ammunition for the soldiers assault rifle or for the M-84 machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I just said that a machine-gun already has bullets stashed in belts. This was just an additional amount for automatic weapons or, rather, automatic rifles that soldiers use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You provided the investigator with some pieces of paper from a -- from one of your notebooks that helped talk about some of the food and ammunition from that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll show you the original pieces of paper and that is -- comes out as Exhibit P02868, but before we get to sort of the details, can you -- this is obviously just one little piece of paper from one of those small notebooks. Can you tell us about this notebook that it came from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this a notebook you actually used during the war or is this something that you prepared for the investigators?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This is an internal notebook, in Momo's absence that was used by soldiers or someone who was my substitute, in case that any inspection would come subsequently, I would have the proof of all the material issued, food and bullets and everything else, materiel, in one word. It's a kind of internal record that is kept in the storehouse, which says who issued something, if I was not there, so these were the entries made there. In my absence, they were noted down, and then I would write it in the proper form in order for any possible inspection coming from the main site to see how much was spent in terms of food and ammunition. I have to have proper records corresponding to the consumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was Momo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Momo is? You mentioned Momo briefly and that's I'm sure -- can you tell us who that is so we understand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe somebody heard that but there was no Momo in the unit. Maybe that was my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least exactly. I mean the transcript says, "This is an internal notebook, in Momo's absence there was used -- that was used" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my absence, when I was away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. That explains it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- well, the proper records you're speaking of, were you able to find any of those records for the -- for the investigators? I mean relating to these -- this sort of material specifically, the --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about my records? My personal records?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, you said there were proper records where you had to write down the ammunition and the food. Do we have any of those?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you find any of those records?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: You can look for that only in Bijeljina because everything was sealed after we had finished combat operation and the war was over, everything was sealed and the handover of materiel and equipment was carried out. Everything was taken to the collection centre in Bijeljina, of all the papers documents and other material. It was meaningless without a proper form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you did manage to find this one page. Did you have a whole notebook when you gave this one page to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had a notebook but I told you this was some kind of internal paper used to issue financial aid to those who were killed, for the burial. So there was just a kind of internal document. The person who happened to be there would just note it down and then I would enter it into a proper form and then my commander had to sign it as well. If there was anything missing or lacking from the stocks, then I would be accused of misappropriating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's just talk about this little internal thing since it's what we have. When you gave this one page to the investigator, did you have the whole book as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you gave that to the investigator, you kept the book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He asked me to do that. He asked me if I could give him that. For me, this is a worthless paper. It doesn't mean anything. It says pate, green peas, oil, sugar, salt. No soldier would take that into the mission. Ammunition that was issued. This was some sort of aid that was given to us by somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- we see that we have a date marked here, 15 July 1995, and then under it is fish, pate, luncheon meat, pepper.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This is a soldier's handwriting. His name is Milesic [Realtime transcript read in error "millcic"], Milovan. He would stand in for me. He lived in Janja. He got ill last year. He died of cancer, I think. He was in charge of these things in Bijeljina like I was in Vlasenica. When I was in the field, he would stand in for me or one of the gate-keepers would. We had four gate-keepers in the units and if I wasn't there, one of them could issue something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very simply, there is a mistake in the examination-in-chief. The witness said "Milesic" and it has been transcribed as "millcic".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milovan Milesic [Realtime transcript in error "millsic"], also known as Malisa. He was from Zenica, from the village of Drinjesa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you both but again in the transcript, we have "millsic". And I think he said Milesic. Yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the best solution would be for the witness to spell because the name is still transcribed incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I said. I could hear him say Milesic. Mr. Todorovic, can you spell for us the family name of this Milovan, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I-L-E-S-I-C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still are missing the M, the first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first letter is M. M-I-L-E-S-I-C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough now. We can proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In looking at this, the document, this 7, 6, 2, AP, can you tell us what that is -- what that means?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This is rifle ammunition for an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then it says, looks like 2 point or 2 comma 400 KG. What's that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: That's a mistake. It could only be KOM. This is 80 packages of ammunition, so it could only be KOM standing for piece. It could only be two boxes. This is a mistake. The KG is a mistake. It could only be 2400 pieces of bullets for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So 2400 rounds of 7.62 ammo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pieces for an automatic rifle. Bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know if this reference which appears to be between the 14th and the 15th by the note, has anything to do with the thing that was going on on the 15th when ammunition and food was being passed out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know. I don't know why this ammunition was issued. I recorded everything correctly, but it was not my place to ask any questions, nor was there anybody to ask for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. I understand that. I'm not worrying about the mission or that. This ammunition, do you remember 2400 rounds of 7.62 going to this group on the 15th? Do you remember that in that kind of detail or do you think this might have to do with something else, maybe on the 14th or something else, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No. I provided that group with one package of ammunition for automatic weapons, just one package of ammunition I provided them with. I provided them with 8 to 10 cold meat packages, water, a machine-gun with the ammunition belts, that are reserve belts that the troops normally don't use before they go out on a mission. I prepared all that for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that but do you think this reference to ammunition and then the food on the 15th is a reflection of what you gave them or at least part of what you gave them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I gave them that on a piece of paper and Franc Kos signed that piece of paper and the size of the paper is like this what I'm showing you, Franc Kos signed that paper because he had a rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand there is a more official document but does this unofficial document reflect the same stuff that would have been on the official document for this day that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Of course. All this was reflected on the official document, and somebody had to sign that paper in order to confirm that things had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you turn over the original and if we can go to the next page in the computer, we -- there is one more entry. It's ERN 938. And does that handwriting appear to be different to you than the previous page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It looks very similar to me. I would not place a bet on this being the same handwriting but it's very similar and the colour of the pen is different but I would say that this is very similar to the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So do you know who may have written this or do you think it's the same person, the deceased person, or could it have been someone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I assume, 90 per cent I'm sure, that it is his handwriting. Only the colour of the ballpoint pen is different. The previous document is different. It's somewhat bolder than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just for the record, when you say, "His," can you give us the name of your friend that's died?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The late Milovan Milesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if we go down that list, now on the 16th, we see luncheon meat, ammunition for M-84, do you know anything about -- well, you know, before I ask you about that, let's get finished with the 15th, okay? And then we'll come back to this. What happens? You described you've -- that Pecanac has an argument with Zoran Obrenovic, Zoran Obrenovic tells you a bit about what is supposed to happen but what actually happens that you see that day at the base?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Nothing unusual happened. The troops left the base, they had been provided with all the logistical support, and they started marching on the road leading towards Sekovici, Tisca, Kladanj. There are several roads there. I didn't ask anybody where they were headed to. I didn't dare ask anybody. I didn't know what their mission was. The commander wasn't there. Without his approval, nobody was allowed to leave the base but the officer took this responsibility upon himself, I suppose, and the troops left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About how many troops from the 10th left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Seven or eight maybe, as many as a minivan could hold together with the driver. I don't know how many people can fit in an APC. Maybe eight. And the APC is 4 because of all the equipment that they were taking with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There may be a translation issue so let me just ask you. Can you describe the vehicle this group left in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was a Volkswagen minivan, black. This was given to us by a civilian. I don't know why. Maybe to avoid any other duty towards the army. It was not up to me to question that. It was a vehicle that was registered to the Republika Srpska army. There is a paper trail of the origin and the destiny of that people [as interpreted]. I did not register it. It was not up to me. My duty was just to fill it with fuel. It was a minivan, a black minivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And was there any vehicle that left at the same time it did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pecanac's vehicle left and the other Golf vehicle that was out there, I don't know whether it was his or not. I didn't see. I can't tell. I suppose that it was his vehicle, of this gentleman. But when you -- if you don't see the driver, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Whether you say, "His," who do you mean? And we understand you're saying you didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: His vehicle, Mr. Popovic's vehicle, but I'm repeating again, I did not see the driver. It would be a mistake to claim something for a fact that you didn't see. It was his vehicle, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand. Okay. You've -- can you tell us some of the soldiers that you -- that left that day in the minivan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Franc Kos, I believe that he took the duty of the leader, although the other one shouted at Brano but Brano did not have a rank. He was a foot soldier. Then there was Gojkovic, I believe. Selanovic. Boris Popov. Marko Boskic. And Mr. Drazen Erdemovic who joined the group a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you actually see these guys go or are you going off a document or someone telling you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I saw the people leave the base and get into the van. Everybody standing at the gate could see that. And I myself had prepared the equipment and all the materiel for the vehicle and the soldiers. Everybody saw them leaving the base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the witness mentioned just now name by Gojkovic. Can I draw your attention to page 50, lines 7 to 9? In answer to your question, the witness is reported to have said, "After Pecanac was giving order to Vojkovic, soldier Vojkovic when he shouted at him." This must be Gojkovic. Could you clarify? And if you could ask the witness to elaborate on this issue, the shouting, yelling, shouting at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First let's clear up who was being shouted at. Was that Brano Gojkovic that got shouted at or someone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Brano.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judge more about that situation, what he was shouting at, at him about, what you could make of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The shouting was about an order that only he was aware of, Pecanac. The whole story was to collect people, to send them out on a mission into the field. What he meant by the mission, whether it was an operation, whether it was securing a person, a road, an elevation, nobody told me anything about that, nor was I allowed to ask where they were going. At that time there was BiH army troops all over the place. They were breaking through and attacking everywhere. I could only assume that they had captured a road, a person or threatened something or somebody. That's why they were sent out of the base. I only know that they left the base, that they had been equipped for a mission but I don't know where they went. I know that Mr. Gojkovic did not have an order, that he didn't have a rank, that he could not command any member of the sabotage unit. He could not issue, he was not in a position to issue any orders to any of the soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Among this group that you've named that left, do you know who was in charge of the group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Franc Kos, who was a second lieutenant signed for the equipment. If hadn't been there it would have been Drazen Erdemovic who would have signed for a document like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had mentioned that Drazen Erdemovic had joined this group a little later. Can you tell us what you know about that, the circumstances about Erdemovic being a member of the group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't want to stay on his own in the base. The intervention squad had already left. Some of the troops were on furlough. Instead of going to Bijeljina on his own, he joined the group that left the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I notice of the group that you remember leaving the base, Erdemovic is the only one of the people that you've named that went all the way to Trebinje and had been driving all the way back that whole night. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He didn't drive. Nebojsa Gagic and Zeljko Vukovic were driving. I didn't say that Erdemovic drove. There were two drivers that went to Trebinje. You'll find it in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... meant that they came back by car. I didn't mean who was behind the wheel. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, they came alive, thank God. They did not carry stones. They were sleeping in the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But Erdemovic was the only one that had gone to Trebinje that went on this mission on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: He volunteered. He wanted to avoid staying on his own in the base. Nobody selected him. Nobody picked him. He volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And after they left, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: With a group of soldiers, I went to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To do what, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: To gather livestock for the unit because we thought at the time that the war would go on for at least a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you come back to the base near Vlasenica that night, the night of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you see when you got back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Everything was okay. The base was calm. All the vehicles were parked. Everything was under control. I unloaded the livestock, tied the cattle that we were to use, and the rest I distributed among the people from whom the livestock had been stolen by Muslims in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see the vehicle that had gone with that group with Pecanac and the other person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was parked to the right from the house, next to a column where the soldiers used to be trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any of the men that had gone on that mission that day that we had talked about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Those who had gone on the mission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Or those with the Slovenian? Those who went with Franc Kos or those who went with me? We are talking about two groups. One went with me to Srebrenica and the others had been taken by --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said you've seen the van that Franc Kos's group took. Did you see the men with Franc Kos? Were they around the base that evening that you saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They went and they came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So Franc Kos and his men were --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They came back before I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So Franc Kos, Erdemovic and that group were back at the base the night of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I suppose they were in town because all the cafes were open. I suppose that they had been given some free time to go into town. I did not see any of them. I just saw the soldier who was on duty, and the gate-keeper who was on duty as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear any information about what they had done that day, which was the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. On the 16th of July, do you see Erdemovic or Franc Kos or Brano Gojkovic or Boskic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of July I was in Srebrenica again. I did not come to the base. I took the same group of people and I took the same truck to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that morning when you left from your base to Srebrenica, though, I take it, the 16th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That morning did you see any of the men I mentioned, Erdemovic, Franc Kos, Brano Gojkovic, Boskic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any mission that they went on that -- you got to let me finish, sorry, we are almost through.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you aware of any mission that those men went on, on the day of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you come back to the base from your Srebrenica trip on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, in the evening, I returned after the mission had been accomplished, and I had done something for the unit. I collected some desks and chairs. We unloaded that. We went home. And the unit was supposed to line up again, either on the 18th or the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What time did you get back to the base on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Again, rather late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That night, did you see Franc Kos, Erdemovic, Boskic or Brano Gojkovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any reliable information on what if anything your -- the 10th Sabotage Detachment did on the 16th of July besides what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I've just told you, I don't really know what the units could have been used for in the absence of the commander. If the commander had been there, I would probably also have known where they were sent. Things were what they were, so they could have been used to secure a road, a higher ranking officer to make the rounds of the line that was kilometres long, maybe one of the officers asked for security or escort. I wasn't there. I don't have anything in writing, anything signed, to tell me where the unit had been sent. If troops are sent somewhere, we would have known that it was either Srebrenica, Vlasenica, Sekovici. This seems to have been the doing of Officer Pecanac, and he alone knew where he was taking these people or so it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's not speculate, and I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. We'll have a break in ten minutes' time. Do you prefer to start now, Mr. Zivanovic, or after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, after the break, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have the break now, 25 minutes, and then we start with the cross-examination. More or less before we break, just to update the time required for cross-examination, I know that you have given, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think we'll reduce our cross-examination estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Approximately 20 to 25 minutes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than ten minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll have no cross-examination whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, I believe I will need about 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Unlikely to have any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If anything at all, five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I represent Vujadin Popovic and I'll have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us at the very beginning that you resided in Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what were your reasons for leaving Kladanj and moving to Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: The reasons were war, avoiding any threats. I chose a different town to live in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you feel threatened by?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was not only me. It was a town where the majority Muslim population. I believe that 80 per cent of the population were Muslim at the time. Certain units had already been established while I was there. It was only normal for me to leave and save my family. Everybody else who left had the same reasons. Those who did not leave or join the BiH army would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us here, amongst other things, and I'm going back to the event that took place on the 15th of July, that the group that was sent out on this mission of which you did not know much, was provided with zoljas as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether you know that the zoljas are normally used only as assault weapon to open fire at tanks, bunkers, dugouts and different things like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would that indicate in your view what the destination of the group was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I inferred from that that it was either an ambush or a road was being blocked. It depended on the situation on the ground, whether the unit would be attacked or whether it would be engaged in attack launched by them. It all depended on the situation. Zolja is used to enforce the machine-gun fire. If the unit is -- comes under attack, if a person has to be provided security for, or if a road is to be secured, if a combat line is to be inspected, this was part of the duty of an officer to inspect combat lines to see what the troops have at their disposal. Every higher ranking officer had to be accompanied by their security when they went on a mission into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I read that you said this in an interview that you had with the investigators of the United States of America, I believe that those were FBI investigators?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you repeat the same thing before the investigator of The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This question, yes. No, nobody asked me about the use of the unit they just asked me about the composition of the unit, who was responsible for the unit, who was responsible person, what was the military post, the command, who was the head of the unit and what was its purpose; and I said that the purpose of the unit was fighting behind the enemy lines and providing security for the facilities and persons, depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, the investigators also asked you whether and what you issued to the group that was sent out on a mission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I told them that I issued them with a PKT, with the ammunition, rucksack for the water, the necessary food and all the personal effects. I didn't know how long they would stay in the field, whether it would be a day, two days or three days. Nobody ever told me that, they just told me that the troops were sent out on a mission, and the normal procedure is to provide them with all the necessity for 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that to the investigators of the Tribunal when they first asked you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that you will find it in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in the statement that you're referring to either by omission or by mistake, it was omitted that you issued the troops with the zoljas?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was omitted in the first statement that I provided the FBI with. Somebody did ask me this thing, the others didn't. I don't know who it was, who asked me and I believe that the FBI investigators didn't ask me about zoljas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I think you're going too fast. Please allow a small pause between question and answer since you speak the same language, and what you say needs to be translated to us. And the interpreters, I can figure out, are finding it a little bit difficult. So Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that you told the FBI investigators and that has been recorded in the statement, that rocket launchers were given to the troops and in the statement that The Hague Tribunal investigators took, it is stated that you issued them with a machine-guns and ammunition, but this is omitted.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked me. If I had been asked, I would have answered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you something else with regard to your contact with the Tribunal investigators on the 14th of June 2005 in Banja Luka. You provided the investigator on that occasion with certain documents. Those documents were taken from you. Among those documents, if you recall, there were some lists of materiel and equipment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This is what every soldier in unit had. When they were enlisted, they were issued with a piece of paper showing what they were issued with. It was like a personal chart, a personal list for every soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to these personal charts, there were some other lists called the exit of goods and materiel, containing all sorts of food-stuff like cold cuts and other similar things. I believe that you will remember this as well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What attracted my attention was the fact that in these reports, it is indicated that you had handed over a number of such documents without any breakdown of those documents, no lists of those documents were ever made. I'm asking you this: Did the investigator ever suggest that something like this should be done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it on a piece of paper. I was given this when I came to testify and that list shows some five or six items of the documents that I had handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Five or six. I believe that we have the same paper that you're now referring to. I would like this to be shown to you and I would like you to tell us whether -- just bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please first look at item 1? This report is in English, though, I don't have a B/C/S translation of this particular page, of this report. I'm going to read it to you so item 1 says, "[In English] Batch of invoices of issued supplies to the VRS 10th Sabotage Detachment to the period July 1995, January 1996." [Interpretation] So in other words, you have handed over a number of records relating to the materiel issued. Now I have found a B/C/S version as well so you can look at it. I'm sure you recall this.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone ask you -- I'm talking about the investigators -- let us make a list of these records and see whether there are some kind of 50 or 100 or 20 receipts of that kind so that we can know exactly what it is that you handed over, I presume it is very difficult for you to remember everything?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I remember very well. There is no problem. I handed over this in Banja Luka and I received this paper only upon my arrival here containing these items, but I know very well, even today, what I gave them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you were not requested on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Neither I requested this nor they.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, Mr. Zivanovic is allowing a pause after your answer but you're not allowing a pause at all after his question. So, please, give the interpreters a chance to translate to us his question before you start answering. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now roughly, from memory, how many papers were there that you handed over?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There were maybe seven or eight personal weapons cards issued to the soldiers. There was a death certificate for Mr. Koljivrat, the member of our unit who was killed. There was an extract from the Vlasenica health centre confirming Dragan Koljivrat's death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us about items 2, 3 and 4 from this list.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: There was a list of troops who were sent out into the field in Srebrenica on the 10th of July. I don't know if the list was made as per establishment, per formation, or in alphabetic order but I think it's irrelevant. And I think there was another list, a kind of peril [as interpreted] or donations from the municipality, the relief that they provided in firewood and things like that but basically it contained probably the names of members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me draw your attention now to item 1, if you can please look at it, I think you have it on your monitor or in front of you. Let us just look at item 1. It says that it's a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is speaking about these documents, I suppose that at the moment you cannot remember exactly how many of these documents were and what kind of documents they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Those were these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you by showing you some of the pieces of paper, although I don't know whether they are all relevant, if you can please take a look. Can you please look at these pieces of paper and say whether these were the documents that you handed over on that specific occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There are quite a few of these papers dating from July all the way to January 1996. I suppose that you cannot remember exactly how many documents of this kind there were.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is precisely what I wanted to hear. You were never asked to prepare a list of these material lists?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Banja Luka the investigator didn't suggest that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, they just asked me if I can give these documents. This is the paper that I used in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. Let me ask you one more thing. You described to us that on the 11th of July, you and your unit were in positions around Srebrenica. Can you tell me whether Srebrenica was being shelled during the time that you were there? Were any shells fired at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: We arrived in Srebrenica when already there were many troops there, since it was night, the night went by calmly, we spent the night outdoors, there was not much shooting and there was no intense shelling, which is otherwise normal when there is an operation in progress. We were at Zeleni Jadar, we were able to see Srebrenica from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see or hear shelling?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. There was just sporadic shooting, nobody took any action during the night. There was no movement of units. Everybody was staying put. There was just an occasional shot fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Meek confirmed that he has no questions. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, just a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Todorovic. Having listening today on page 60, lines 8 to 14 in the transcript, you mentioned a black vehicle. Was that a van?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what other kinds of vehicles did your unit have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: We had a WV [as interpreted] Golf; a red Mitsubishi; a minivan, olive-drab colour; a military vehicle; a Fiat Ritmo, which was a civilian vehicle used by the military; there was another yellow van used to -- for transportation of food. There was a driver from Sekovici who was collecting donations in Serbia or elsewhere, or from local people, so it was also used for transporting soldiers who wanted to move. So their personal belongings were taken in that van and I'm not sure whether there was another truck, 110 or 150.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 14th of July, you testified that you were in Trebinje attending the funeral of the colleague of yours who was killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were a few members of the detachment with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As for other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, you don't know their whereabouts on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know and I didn't have any communication lines with them. We didn't have any communication devices because this is pretty far from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that a group of people from Vlasenica were on leave because their houses were there, and they had a certain rash on their skin so some were sent either to the first aid station in Vlasenica, whereas those from Bijeljina remained in Dragasevac to take a bath and to spend the night there because we had billeting quarters prepared there. And a number of men were with me in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In addition to what you told us about Trebinje and these are just your suppositions, is that they spent the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You're back. Please allow a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. I'm going to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So please wait until I've finished and then give me the answer after that. Apart from the group that was with you in Trebinje, you supposed that other members of the detachments were in the places that you mentioned on page 77, lines 10 to 15 in the previous answer that you gave me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The vehicles that you had, that you mentioned, you also have no knowledge whether they were involved in any missions, I'm talking about the red car, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether these vehicles were being used either by our unit or if they were requisitions or seconded to another unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Nikolic. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we show the witness Exhibit number 2868?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood you well, this is one of the documents that you have handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you got hold of this document in the first place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: How I got hold of the document? This is a document that was drafted in my unit, in my storage where I worked. This is an internal document that I used to transfer the data from it to the paper that counsel Zivanovic showed to me. I believe that's the name of the lawyer who examined me before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But this is a document that originates from your unit but it is not your personal document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This is an internal document which is used in the depot. Anybody can use it, for example, gate-keepers or soldiers who were present, to record what was handed out by way of materiel and technical equipment while I was absent.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this did not had to be archived together with the other documents that originated from the unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: It was archived but I don't know where the original is, I don't know whether it was in Bijeljina when the unit was dismantled, whether it was handed over to somebody else or whether it is stored together with the other archive of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell me where did you obtain this copy of this document or when did you make a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This copy was made by the Tribunal. I had the original. I handed the original over to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And how did you obtain the original?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I had it. This is an internal piece of document that means nothing to anybody. It only served me to transfer on to an official document what was handed over on the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that this document does not mention the 10th Sabotage Unit that was part of your larger unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that originates for the 10th Sabotage Detachment although it indicates the Special Police Sekovici. I got it from a member of the police that I shared the unit with and the heading at the top doesn't mean anything. This document originates from the sabotage detachment. This is my document. It was issued in my unit in the depot where I worked, that I was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to show you another exhibit. P2869 is the number of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the signature part of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The signature on the document is by Mr. Kos, not by Mr. Pelemis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know why Pelemis didn't sign this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've told us earlier today, on page 15, line 19, that Andrija Borovic was his deputy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Bodirogic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know why his deputy didn't sign the document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe he wasn't there. Maybe he was not in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How did you know that Franc Kos was authorised to sign this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I look at the ranks and the highest rank is the person that I address.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to go into private session for the next couple of questions, if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I will no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were in Srebrenica on the 11th of July 1995, were you anywhere close to Drazen Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So that leaves you, Mr. Sarapa. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Would you agree with the assertion that the 10th Sabotage Detachment had 7.62 millimetre submachine-guns and M-84 machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it true that an M-84 signifies the year of production, and that it has nothing to do with calibre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the year, 1984, and the calibre is 7.62.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So it's the same calibre like an automatic rifle, 7.62?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Only the charge is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: But the calibre is the same?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it true that members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment had combat vests and that they had pockets on these vests where they could store ammunition?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: They had combat vests but they also had combat racks that they carried on their right thighs and on the left thighs they carried protective masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So in any event, their uniform was such that with them they were able to carry enough ammunition that constituted the combat kit.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Each member of the detachment had a combat kit consisting of 150 rounds of ammunition, two or three grenades and also depending on the particular situation, they were issued with zolja or with an M-84, that is to say PKT. Frequently, the practice was to load these kind of weapons on the back of the vehicle, just in case it might be needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Is it true that a combat kit for an M-84 machine-gun consists of 600 rounds in belts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether it's part of the kit or whether it's how many rounds can be fired in a minute. I'm not an expert but I believe that 600 rounds is a minimum amount for this type of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So if a unit is issued with a machine-gun and the ammunition for it, do you think that 600 rounds is a minimum amount of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: On that occasion, you issued this group of people with a machine-gun and everything else that you mentioned during your testimony. You also said that they gave them an additional crate with about 1200 rounds for automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Since there was another 1200 rounds for a PKT, I just added one more crate for them to be encounter the situation on the ground, because one crate of PKT ammunition is not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So if we presume that in the crate that you gave them, there was additional 1200 rounds for automatic rifle, and if there were eight men in this group, that means that each one of them was issued with 150 rounds. That would be standard issue for a combat kit. That makes the total of 2400 rounds. If we take the minimum number of rounds required for a machine-gun of the 600, would you agree that that would make a minimum of 3.000 rounds?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: More or less so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You said that Pecanac had insisted on what you spoke in great detail, we are not going to repeat this.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Pecanac was not a direct subordinate to the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So formally speaking, he didn't have an authority to issue any orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: However, his orders were followed through based on his personal assistance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Is there any re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Mr. Todorovic, there are no further questions for you, which means your testimony comes to an end here. You'll be assisted by our staff and before you leave the courtroom, on behalf of my colleagues and on behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having come over and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your hospitality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the next witness here, Mr. McCloskey? I suppose, I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. I cut their estimate in half and that still came up with letting him go. So I -- we let him go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is understandable. Is there anything that maybe the matter that I raised earlier on this morning about the guidelines? Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Not on that issue, Your Honour, but I see-- I think there is a problem with line 25, page 84. Mr. Sarapa asked the question so normally speaking he didn't have authority and the transcript says normally speaking I didn't have the authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need to get the witness back or not? I don't think so. I mean it's -- okay. We can live with that. Is there any further business you wish or you are in a position to transact, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe we -- well, of course the exhibits, but I believe we have spoken to the Popovic team about the issue we had spoken of, but Mr. Nicholls said we might have had something resolved but I can see from the looks not quite yet. But we'll resolve that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's get the exhibits, then. We conclude that. Do you have any exhibits? I suppose so, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, the three that are on the list that we spoke of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. They are so tendered and I guess I will give them the proper identification number. Defence? Madam Fauveau? You wish to tender any documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That basically brings this to an end. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could just note that it's P02867, 68 and 69 that would help Ms. Stewart and our records to keep track of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Then I think we can adjourn until tomorrow. All right. You do not anticipate any problems in relation to the next witness? Okay. Thank you.
